title: Can readers understand findings from systematic reviews almost as well from artificial intelligence-assisted visual abstracts as from those published by The BMJ?
official: Comparison of AI-assisted visual abstracts and published BMJ visual abstracts for systematic reviews: protocol for a non-inferiority randomised trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Systematic reviews bring together the results of many studies to answer a healthcare question. They are useful but are often long and technical. Visual abstracts use short text and simple graphics to show the main points more quickly and clearly, but making them takes time and design skill.
Artificial intelligence (AI) could help, but it can also make mistakes, leave out how certain or uncertain the evidence is, or present findings in a misleading way. Our study tests a structured way of working that aims to reduce these risks. AI will produce a first draft from a fixed set of written instructions. Two researchers experienced in systematic reviews will check each draft against the original review and correct any problems.
Our main question is whether readers understand the information almost as well from the AI-assisted visual abstracts as from visual abstracts published by The BMJ.

Who can participate?
We will recruit 656 adults aged 18 years or older, of any sex, who have relevant professional, academic, policy-related, or actively engaged healthcare or research experience. This may include clinicians, health researchers, public health professionals, systematic review authors or users, guideline developers, policymakers, healthcare decision makers, and eligible patient, caregiver, or peer-research partners actively involved in healthcare or research initiatives.
Participants must be able to read and understand English, have internet access and a suitable device, and provide electronic informed consent. People who helped select, develop, anonymise, pilot, or pretest the visual abstracts used in the trial cannot participate.

What does the study involve?
A computer will randomly decide whether each participant sees three AI-assisted visual abstracts or three visual abstracts already published by The BMJ. Both sets will cover the same three systematic reviews.
After each visual abstract, participants will answer six questions about the information shown and rate its clarity and trustworthiness. Each participant will complete these assessments online in a single session.
Separately, the research team will assess the reading level of the text. Independent experts will compare the final visual abstracts in both groups with their source reviews and judge whether they could mislead readers. They will also compare each first uncorrected AI-generated draft with its source review and record the types, number, and locations of any errors.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants should not expect a direct personal or clinical benefit. Their responses may help researchers improve how findings from systematic reviews are communicated. The study does not involve medical treatment or physical procedures. The main burdens are the time and concentration needed to view the materials and answer the questions, and possible tiredness or frustration while completing the online assessments.

Where is the study run from?
The study is managed by the Centre for Health Research Methodology at the University of Galway, Ireland. Participants will be recruited internationally through Prolific and will complete all procedures remotely from their own locations.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to March 2027.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the University of Galway (Ireland).

Who is the main contact?

conditions: Health information communication and comprehension of findings from systematic reviews presented in visual abstracts.

interventions.name:
This study is a randomised, parallel-group, two-arm, non-inferiority trial among international healthcare interest holders. It compares visual abstracts produced through a prespecified, checklist-informed, human-verified AI-assisted workflow with the selected visual abstracts published by The BMJ.
P

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. An international healthcare interest holder, defined for this trial as an individual with professional, academic, or policy-related experience in healthcare, clinical practice, public health, health research, evidence synthesis, guideline development, health technology assessment, journal publishing, or healthcare policy. Eligible groups may include clinicians, health researchers, public health professionals, systematic review authors or users, guideline developers, policymakers, healthcare decision makers, patient/caregiver or peer-research partners actively involved in healthcare or research initiatives, and professionals involved in evidence-informed healthcare practice or policy, provided they meet the experience-based definition above
2. Aged 18 years or older
3. Of any sex
4. Able to read and understand English sufficiently to engage with the visual abstract materials and complete the study assessments. Participants must report English as their native or first language or select Fluent, Advanced, or Mastery on the adapted Common European Framework of Reference for Languages-based screening item
5. Access to the internet and to a computer, tablet, smartphone, or other device capable of displaying the visual abstract materials and completing the online study procedures
6. Able and willing to provide electronic informed consent before participation
Exclusion criteria:
Previous participation in the selection, development, anonymisation, piloting, or pretesting of the visual abstract materials used in the trial
